slides.kicker: PUBLIC LECTURE · MINDS, BRAINS AND SELVES
slides.title: The Philosophy of Mind
slides.question: How can three pounds of brain feel anything at all?
slides.sub: Consciousness, the mind–body problem, other minds, machine minds and the self
slides.notes:
Your brain weighs about a kilogram and a half. It is made of the same atoms as a rock or a cup of tea. Yet somehow, right now, it is producing the experience of reading these words: the colours, the sounds, the feeling of being you. How?
That is the question tonight. Philosophy of mind asks what minds are, how they relate to bodies, how we know other people have them, whether machines could, and what a self is. Science has told us an enormous amount about the brain. Whether it has explained the mind is exactly what is in dispute.
Next: the problem in its sharpest form.

slides.title: Explaining what the brain does is easy; explaining why it feels like something is hard

cols.label: The ‘easy’ problems
cols.title: How the brain works
cols.text: How we see edges, recognise faces, remember, report and act. Hard in practice, but the kind of problem science solves: find the mechanism.

cols.label: The hard problem
cols.title: Why there’s an inside
cols.text: Why is all that processing accompanied by experience at all? Why does red look like this, and pain feel like that, rather than happening in the dark?

slides.bottom: Even a complete map of the brain might leave one question open: why is there something it is like to be you?
slides.notes:
David Chalmers distinguished the easy problems from the hard problem. The easy ones are not easy at all, but they are about mechanisms: how the brain processes colour, stores memories or steers attention. Science handles that kind of question well.
The hard problem is different. Imagine you knew every fact about neurons firing when someone looks at a red rose. Would you know why there is a red experience, rather than just processing? Many think not. Others, like Daniel Dennett, think the ‘hard problem’ is an illusion that will dissolve once the easy problems are solved.
Next: a famous argument that experience is something extra.

slides.title: What is it like to be a bat? Facts about experience seem to escape physical description

challenge.title: Two thought experiments
challenge.text: Bats navigate by echolocation. You could learn every physical fact about a bat’s sonar, yet still not know what it is like to be one.

answer.title: Mary’s room
answer.text: Mary is a brilliant scientist who knows every physical fact about colour vision, but has lived all her life in a black-and-white room. When she first sees a red rose, does she learn something new? If so, not all facts are physical.

open.title: Physicalist replies
open.text: Mary gains a new ability or a new way of knowing an old fact, not a new fact (Lewis, Churchland). Or she could already work it out (Dennett).

slides.bottom: If Mary learns something new, physics can’t be the whole story; if she doesn’t, explain the gasp.
slides.notes:
Thomas Nagel asked what it is like to be a bat. Bats ‘see’ by sonar, and no amount of physical information seems to tell you what that is like from the inside. Frank Jackson made the point sharper with Mary, the colour scientist in a black-and-white room. When she steps out and sees red, she seems to learn something. If she already knew all the physical facts, the new thing she learns must be non-physical.
Physicalists have replies: Mary gains an ability, not a fact, or a new way of representing a fact she already knew. Jackson himself later changed his mind and became a physicalist. You can try the experience yourself in Mary’s Room in the Shipyard.
Next: the main answers to how mind relates to body.

slides.title: Four main answers to how mind and body are related

cols.label: Substance dualism
cols.title: Two kinds of thing
cols.text: Descartes: the mind is a non-physical thing that thinks; the body is a machine. They interact.
cols.note: Problem: how does a non-physical mind push neurons?

cols.label: Physicalism
cols.title: Only the physical
cols.text: The mind is what the brain does. Mental states are brain states (Smart, Churchland) or functional roles (Putnam).

cols.label: Property dualism
cols.title: One thing, two kinds of property
cols.text: Only brains, but brains have non-physical properties: experiences (Chalmers).

cols.label: Panpsychism
cols.title: Mind is everywhere
cols.text: Experience is a basic feature of all matter; brains organise it (Goff, and many ancient traditions).
cols.note: Problem: how do tiny minds combine?

slides.bottom: Each view solves one puzzle by creating another: choose which puzzle you can live with.
slides.linkLabel: Take your stand in My Positions
slides.notes:
René Descartes thought the mind was a separate, non-physical substance. Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia asked him the decisive question in 1643: how can something without extension or position move a body? He never gave a satisfying answer.
Most philosophers today are physicalists: the mind is the brain at work. Some identify mental states with brain states; functionalists like Hilary Putnam say mental states are defined by what they do, so the same mind could in principle run on silicon.
Property dualists say there is only the brain, but it has special properties, experiences, that physics leaves out. Panpsychists go further: experience in some simple form belongs to all matter.
Next: what philosophers actually believe.

slides.title: Where professional philosophers stand
slides.caption: Mind: physicalism or non-physicalism?
slides.text: About 52% accepted or leaned towards physicalism and about 32% towards non-physicalism, with the rest undecided or holding other views. The question is genuinely open among experts.
slides.notes:
The PhilPapers survey asks professional philosophers where they stand on major questions. In 2020 about half leaned towards physicalism and about a third towards non-physicalism. That is a real split among people who have studied the question for decades. You are not behind if you are unsure.
Next: how do you know anyone else has a mind at all?

slides.title: You only ever feel your own feelings: how do you know anyone else has any?

cols.label: Analogy
cols.title: They’re like me
cols.text: Their bodies behave like mine when I’m in pain, so they probably feel pain too (Mill).

cols.label: Best explanation
cols.title: Minds explain behaviour
cols.text: Inner lives are the best explanation of what people say and do, as electrons explain experiments.

cols.label: Common sense
cols.title: No proof needed
cols.text: Belief in other minds is basic and reasonable without argument, like trusting memory (Reid).

cols.label: Scepticism
cols.title: I can’t know
cols.text: A perfect mimic would look the same; strictly, you could be the only mind there is.

slides.bottom: We are all confident others feel; the puzzle is explaining what entitles us to be.
slides.notes:
You see someone stub a toe and wince. You never feel their pain, only see their face. So how do you know there is pain there? John Stuart Mill argued by analogy from your own case, but that is a generalisation from one example. Others say minds are the best explanation of behaviour. Thomas Reid said we don’t need an argument: it is a basic belief we are entitled to. And a sceptic will point out that, strictly, nothing you observe proves anyone else feels anything.
Next: this question becomes urgent with machines.

slides.title: Could a machine think, or only seem to?

a.name: The Turing test
a.label: Alan Turing · 1950
a.lead: Forget ‘can machines think?’ Ask whether a machine can converse so well that you can’t tell it from a person.
points: If behaviour is all we have for other humans, why demand more of machines?
Functionalism: mind is what a system does, not what it’s made of

b.name: The Chinese room
b.label: John Searle · 1980
b.lead: A man who knows no Chinese follows a rulebook to answer Chinese questions perfectly. Does he understand Chinese?
points: Syntax is not enough for meaning

slides.bottom: Today’s chatbots make an old thought experiment into a live question.
slides.notes:
Alan Turing proposed replacing the vague question ‘can machines think?’ with a test: if a machine can hold a conversation indistinguishable from a person’s, we have as much reason to say it thinks as we do for other people.
John Searle replied with the Chinese room. A man in a room follows instructions to manipulate Chinese symbols and produces perfect answers, without understanding a word. That, Searle said, is all a computer does.
Replies: perhaps the whole system, man plus rulebook, understands. Large language models now make this debate practical. Do they understand, or only seem to?
Next: what is the self that has a mind?

slides.title: What makes you the same person over time?

challenge.title: The case
challenge.text: A machine scans you, destroys your body, and builds a perfect copy on Mars with all your memories. Did you travel, or die?

answer.title: Three answers
answer.text: Psychological view (Locke): you are your continuing memories and personality, so you survived. Animal view (Olson): you are this living organism, so you died. Soul view: you are a non-physical self that may or may not come along.

open.title: Parfit’s twist
open.text: What if the scanner fails to destroy the original? Now there are two. Derek Parfit concluded that identity isn’t what matters; continuity of mind is.

slides.bottom: Puzzles about copying suggest ‘same person’ may not be an all-or-nothing fact.
slides.notes:
John Locke argued that personal identity consists in consciousness and memory: you are the same person as whoever’s experiences you can remember. On that view the teleported copy is you. Animalists like Eric Olson say you are a biological organism, and organisms don’t survive being destroyed.
Derek Parfit pushed further. If the original survives too, there are two equally good candidates. Since both can’t be you, perhaps identity isn’t what matters. What matters is that someone carries on your memories, plans and loves.
Next: traditions that say there is no self at all.

slides.title: Is there a self at all? Answers from many traditions
slides.sub: From a soul to a story to no self

items.caption: Descartes
items.text: A thinking thing: ‘I think, therefore I am’

items.caption: Hume
items.text: A bundle of perceptions; no self found when I look inward

items.caption: The Buddha
items.text: Anattā: no unchanging self, only a stream of processes

items.caption: Shankara
items.text: Atman: pure awareness, identical with ultimate reality

items.caption: Metzinger
items.text: The self is a model the brain builds

items.caption: A river
items.text: Real, but never the same water: the self as process

slides.bottom: ‘No self’ rarely means ‘you don’t exist’: it means nothing unchanging sits behind your experiences.
slides.notes:
When David Hume looked inward for his self, he found only particular perceptions, never a self having them. The Buddha taught anattā, no-self, two thousand years earlier: what we call ‘I’ is a changing stream of body, feelings, perceptions and thoughts. Shankara, in the Advaita Vedanta tradition, said the opposite: the true self, atman, is pure awareness and is identical with Brahman, ultimate reality. Thomas Metzinger argues the self is a model the brain constructs.
Notice that ‘no self’ views don’t say you don’t exist. Like a river, you are real, but you are a process, not a thing.
Next: the whole field on one page.

slides.title: Philosophy of mind is a map of trade-offs
slides.sub: Every view pays a price somewhere
head: Question
Main answers
The price
rows: How do we know other minds?
Yes, if they function right · No, syntax isn’t meaning
slides.bottom: Knowing the price of each answer is more useful than picking one too soon.
slides.notes:
Here is the field on one page. Every answer pays a price somewhere. That is not a weakness of philosophy; it’s an honest map of a genuinely hard problem.
Next: a toolkit for thinking about minds.

slides.title: Four questions for any claim about minds

steps.title: Easy or hard?
steps.text: Is this about mechanism, or about why it feels like something?

steps.title: From the inside or outside?
steps.text: Is the evidence behaviour, or experience?

steps.title: Could it be multiplied?
steps.text: What happens if it’s copied, split or simulated?

steps.title: What would change your mind?
steps.text: Which discovery would count against your view?

slides.bottom: Most confusion about minds comes from mixing up the mechanism with the experience.
slides.notes:
Four questions. Is this claim about how something works, or why it feels like anything? Is the evidence from outside or inside? What happens in copying or splitting cases? And what would make you change your mind?
Next: what the field leaves us with.

slides.title: Philosophy of mind leaves us with the deepest mystery we carry around
questions: Why does any physical process feel like something?
Could a machine you talk to be someone?
Will the person waking up tomorrow be you?
slides.line: Every other question in philosophy is asked by a mind; this one asks what that is.
slides.notes: Every other question in philosophy is asked by a mind. This field asks what the asker is.

slides.title: Discussion: bring the theory back to real life
questions: If an AI said it was suffering, what would it take for you to believe it?
Should we worry about the experiences of octopuses and insects?
Would you step into the teleporter?
slides.line: Say what you think a mind is first, then answer.
slides.notes: Three questions. Start by saying what you think a mind is, then see where your answer takes you.
